title: Checking it doesn't make things up: your question set
promise: You'll build an exam of twenty questions with their correct answers and put the system through it, so you have a number instead of an impression. By the end you'll know which kinds of question you can trust it on and which you can't, and you'll be able to repeat the exam every time you change something.
why: Nuria signed off on her system because «the answers came out right». When she finally sat down to test it properly with thirty questions she knew the answers to, she got twenty-one. Of the nine it failed, seven were questions about things that had changed over the years. It wasn't a general problem: it was a very specific hole, in a very specific kind of question. Without the exam she'd have carried on believing it was going «pretty well» and carried on sending expired facts to her clients. The exam didn't make her system worse: it told her where not to trust it.

theory.title: «It's going pretty well» is not a measurement
theory.text: Everyone evaluates these setups the same way: they ask five questions, the answers look right, and they take it as working. The problem is that the five questions that occur to you off the cuff are almost always the same kind, the easy kind: facts written plainly in a single recent document. The failures don't live there. They live in the questions that cross two documents, in the ones touching something that changed, and in the ones with no answer at all. An exam written in advance, with the kinds deliberately spread out, gives you a number and tells you where the hole is. And the most valuable part: you can repeat it. Every time you add documents or change the instructions, you run the same exam again and see whether you improved or broke something.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between «the car runs fine» and an MOT. The first is a feeling; the second tells you what's failing and lets you compare it with last year's.
theory.example: Nuria: 21 out of 30. But split by kind, it was 14 out of 15 on direct facts and 2 out of 9 on things that had changed. That second number was the one that mattered.

theory.title: The five classes of question you have to include
theory.text: An exam that's worth anything has all five, and four questions of each is plenty. The first class is the direct fact: it's written in full in one document. The second is the fact you have to piece together from two documents. The third is a question about something that changed over time, where the correct answer is the current version. The fourth, the most important, is questions with no answer: things that aren't in any document of yours, where getting it right means saying «I don't have it». And the fifth is ambiguous questions, the ones that can be read two ways, where the right behaviour is to ask what you mean rather than pick one.
theory.example: Direct: «What's my registration deadline?» Piecing together: «What terms do I have with Ferretería Beltrán and since when?» Changed: «What's the surcharge for late filing?» No answer: «What's my protocol for workplace-accident leave?» Ambiguous: «What do I charge Martínez?», when three of your clients are called Martínez.

theory.title: The correct answer is written first, not afterwards
theory.text: This seems obvious and almost nobody does it. If you write the correct answer after seeing what the system said, your judgement is already contaminated: you'll settle. The correct answer gets written before you ask, with the file it's in, and then it isn't touched. Then you compare. And there's one more rule that saves you arguing with yourself: decide in advance what counts as correct. What's reasonable is that the fact has to be right and the source has to be right. If it gets the fact right but cites a file that doesn't contain it, that isn't a hit: it's a hit by accident, and by accident it will also miss.
theory.example: On Nuria's sheet, each row has four columns: the question, the correct answer, the file it's in, and which of the five classes it belongs to. Nothing else.

theory.title: Splitting the exam by kind is what gives you the diagnosis
theory.text: 70% overall doesn't tell you what to fix. 93% on direct facts and 22% on things that changed tells you exactly where the problem is and what to do: in that case, add status labels and pull out the expired documents. Every kind of failure points to a different fix. If direct facts fail, the problem is search or documents that didn't upload. If the piecing-together ones fail, it's usually that the question needs splitting in two. If the change ones fail, it's status labels. If the no-answer one fails, it's instructions. And if the ambiguous one fails, you need to tell it to ask when it's unsure.
theory.example: Nuria fixed the status labels on 40 documents and pulled out 15 expired ones. She ran the same exam again: she went from 2 out of 9 to 8 out of 9 on that kind. Two hours of work, measured.

theory.title: What to do with what you can't fix
theory.text: After two rounds of fixes you'll be left with a remainder that fails and you don't know why. That's normal and it doesn't mean the setup is bad. What you do isn't keep fighting: you write it down. A short note saying «this system is reliable on X, has to be checked by hand on Y, and isn't any use for Z». That note is worth more than one more percentage point, because it's what tells you when you can forward an answer to a client without looking and when you can't. A system with known limits is useful. A system you believe always gets it right is dangerous.
theory.example: Nuria's note: «Reliable for my own criteria and client terms. Always check any official deadline or surcharge by hand. No use for accounts or adding up amounts.»

theory.title: Repeating it is what makes it valuable
theory.text: The exam isn't a one-day thing. Its value is that you run it again every time something changes: when you upload new documents, when you touch the instructions, when you switch tools or when the company providing it updates its model, which happens without telling you. That's when you discover something that used to work has stopped working, which is a failure you'd otherwise not see until it blew up in front of a client. Twenty questions take about a quarter of an hour.
theory.example: Nuria runs it on the first Monday of each month and whenever she uploads a batch of documents. In March she dropped from 27 to 22 without touching anything: the model underneath had changed. She found out in fifteen minutes rather than through an angry client.

tasks.title: Build the exam sheet
tasks.where: In a spreadsheet or a table
tasks.action: Create a table with five columns: Question, Correct answer, File it's in, Kind, and Result. In Kind you'll put one of these five words: direct, piecing, changed, no-answer, ambiguous. Leave it empty for now and save it next to your working folder.
tasks.expect: An empty table with five columns. Not a single row yet: structure first, so you don't end up writing twenty questions of the same kind.
tasks.stuck: If you don't use spreadsheets, a document with a list works. The only thing that matters is that the Kind column is there, because it's what gives you the diagnosis.

tasks.title: Write four questions of each kind
tasks.action: Twenty rows, four of each kind. Fill in the question, the correct answer and the file, all before asking the system anything. For the «no-answer» kind you have to invent reasonable questions for your sector that you know aren't in any of your documents; there the correct answer is «it isn't in my documents». For the ambiguous ones, look for real cases from your work: two clients with the same surname, two products with similar names, a term that means two different things depending on context.
tasks.expect: Twenty complete rows minus the Result column. It'll take you between thirty and forty-five minutes, and it's the best-invested stretch of the whole block.
tasks.stuck: If the «piecing» ones won't come, think of questions starting «what terms do I have with…?» or «what did we agree with… and since when?». They almost always need a contract and a later email.

tasks.title: Run it end to end without fixing anything on the way
tasks.action: Ask the twenty questions, one at a time, each in a new conversation so it doesn't lean on the previous one. Fill in only the Result column with hit, miss, or «fact right, source wrong». Don't fix anything while you run it, even when you can see the problem clearly: if you change things halfway through, the result isn't comparable afterwards.
tasks.expect: Twenty results. Add up the hits and, above all, split them by kind: four small numbers tell you far more than one big one.
tasks.stuck: If it's dragging, stop at ten questions today and finish tomorrow, but note which row you stopped at. What you can't do is change the instructions between the two sittings.

tasks.title: Have the AI read your results
tasks.where: In a separate chat, not in your project
tasks.action: Paste your filled-in table into a new chat (a normal one, without your documents) and ask for the diagnosis. Careful: strip out any client data from the table first if you're pasting it somewhere you'd rather it didn't appear.
tasks.prompt:
I'm giving you the results of an exam I ran on a system that queries my own documents. Each row has: question, correct answer, file it's in, kind of question, and result.

Tell me, in this order and without flourishes:
1. The hit rate for each kind of question, as a table.
2. Which kind has the worst result and which cause best explains it, choosing from these four: documents that weren't uploaded, missing date and status labels, instructions that don't ban filling gaps, or questions that need splitting in two.
3. The three things I'd fix first, ordered by what raises the hit rate most for the least work.

Don't encourage me and don't give me general conclusions. If the cause of something can't be determined from this data, say so.

RESULTS:
[PASTE YOUR TABLE HERE]
tasks.expect: A table by kind and three concrete fixes. Typically the worst kind is «changed» or «no-answer», and both have quick fixes.
tasks.stuck: If you get a vague diagnosis like «improve document quality», say: «Be more specific: tell me exactly which files from the third column you'd review and what they're missing.»

tasks.title: Apply the first fix and rerun the exam
tasks.where: In your documents or instructions, then in the project
tasks.action: Do only the first of the three fixes, not all three. Then run the same exam again from the start, without changing a single question, and note the new result next to the old one. Doing one fix at a time is the only thing that tells you whether that fix worked; if you do three at once and it improves, you don't know which of the three it was.
tasks.expect: Two columns of results to compare. If the fix was the right one, the kind that was failing rises clearly. If nothing rises, the cause was something else: go back to the diagnosis and try the second.
tasks.stuck: If some kind that was fine drops, look at what you changed in the instructions: sometimes a new rule overrides another. Go back and phrase it differently.

tasks.title: Write down what it's for and what it isn't
tasks.where: In a file next to your working folder
tasks.action: With the numbers in front of you, write five lines: which questions you trust without checking, which you always check by hand, which it isn't any use for, today's date and the exam result. Save it as «what-its-for.txt».
tasks.expect: Five lines. This file is the real deliverable of the block: it's what turns a setup that's «going pretty well» into a tool you know exactly what to expect from.
tasks.stuck: If you're unsure where to draw the line, use this rule: if you get fewer than nine out of ten right on that kind of question, it goes on the always-check-by-hand list. And if it's under half, it goes on the not-any-use list.

matters: That «going pretty well» isn't a measurement and hides exactly the failures that matter.
That there are five kinds of question and the ones with no answer teach you the most.
That the correct answer gets written before you ask, or you end up settling.
That the exam's value is in repeating it: systems get worse on their own when the model underneath changes.
ignore: The metrics with proper names from technical articles. Hits by kind serves you just as well.
Automatic evaluation tools. Twenty questions by hand is plenty.
Chasing 100%. It doesn't exist, and believing you've reached it is worse than knowing your limits.
canDo: Measure your system with a number per kind of question instead of an impression.
Know which fix raises the hit rate, because you tested them one at a time.
Spot that something has got worse without you touching it.
Write down what you can trust it for and what you can't.
cantDo: Spot failures in kinds of question you didn't put in the exam.
Know whether a rule changed: the exam measures the system, not reality.
Skip reading the answers before you send them to a client.
words: The fixed group of questions with their correct answers that you always use to measure the same thing.
One that isn't in any document of yours. Getting it right means saying «I don't have it».
The percentage split by class of question. It's what tells you what to fix.
Something that used to work stopping working. It happens on its own when the model underneath changes.
Getting the answer right while citing a file that doesn't contain it. It doesn't count as a hit: it got there by accident.
next: That closes the data block: your documents queryable, answering with sources, and an exam that tells you what to trust. The next block applies this same way of working to everything else you build: check before treating something as done, and know what you do when it breaks.
